summary: Erik Hanchett presents spec-driven development as a solution to AI coding assistants going off the rails on complex tasks. The core idea is writing structured specifications and design documents in markdown before any code is written, giving large language models the context they need. Hanchett compares AI assistants to eager interns: without proper guidance, they chase random ideas. He outlines caveats: manage context carefully (the Goldilocks zone for agents.md/steering docs), use skills (on-demand instruction files activated by keywords), and never fully trust the agent—you remain the human in the loop, responsible for reviewing all generated code and documents for inconsistencies, hallucinations, and errors. AWS released Kiro, an AI IDE and CLI with vibe and spec modes, which went viral with tens of thousands of downloads. The workflow has three phases: requirements in EARS format with clarifying Q&A, a design document with mermaid diagrams and ASCII art, and implementation tasks. Hanchett recommends stopping after design to inject your own expertise. The implementation phase generates a task list with property-based tests that validate against requirements and design documents. A key tip is asking the AI to pull the top four tasks into an MVP first to see something working. Hanchett also discusses Model Context Protocol (MCP), which lets model providers connect to external data sources like Jira or Asana, pulling product managers' requirements into the spec-driven flow. MCP is still maturing, especially around security, but is valuable for integration. He demos Kiro on a greenfield movie database project, showing design docs with mermaid sequence diagrams, EARS-format requirements, MVP task lists, and property-based tests using fast-check in TypeScript. The approach works for both greenfield and legacy projects.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Spec-driven development means writing structured specifications and design documents in markdown before any code is written.
AI coding assistants are like eager interns—they need explicit guidance and context to avoid going off the rails.
The workflow has three phases: requirements (EARS format), design document, and implementation tasks with property-based tests.
Always review generated markdown files for inconsistencies, hallucinations, and errors—you are the human in the loop.
A practical tip: ask the AI to create an MVP from the top few tasks first so you can see it working before full implementation.
Property-based tests validate implementation against requirements and design documents, running dozens or hundreds of times with different values.
Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables pulling requirements from project management tools like Jira or Asana into the spec-driven flow.
MCP is still maturing, especially around security, but is worth watching for integration opportunities.
AWS released Kiro (IDE and CLI) with spec mode; it went viral with tens of thousands of downloads.
Spec-driven development works for both greenfield and existing legacy projects, not just new ones.

sections.title: Introduction and Definition of Spec-Driven Development
sections.summary: Hanchett introduces spec-driven development as creating structured specifications in markdown before any code is written, emphasizing it improves both speed and code quality when used with AI coding assistants.

sections.title: Why Spec-Driven Development: The AI Interns Analogy
sections.summary: Compares AI coding assistants to eager interns who need guidance, sharing a personal anecdote about dropping everything for a VP's random ideas. Spec-driven development helps keep AI on track.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction
sections.summary: Erik Hanchett introduces himself as a Senior Developer Advocate at AWS with 15+ years of software development experience, inviting connections on LinkedIn.

sections.title: Why Frontier Models Aren't Enough
sections.summary: Addresses whether frontier models can do everything already. Models are improving but still not perfect; more context helps guide them. Some harnesses are adding thinking/planning modes, but human-authored documents remain superior.

sections.title: Key Considerations: Context, Skills, and Trust
sections.summary: Covers three caveats: manage context carefully (Goldilocks zone for agents.md/steering docs), use skills (on-demand instruction files activated by keywords), and maintain trust as the human in the loop responsible for code review.

sections.title: AWS History and Kiro Release
sections.summary: Describes AWS's observation of customers using bespoke spec patterns, leading to the release of Kiro (IDE and CLI) in general availability. Kiro features vibe and spec modes, went viral with tens of thousands of downloads, and is available at kiro.dev.

sections.title: How to Do Spec-Driven Development
sections.summary: Explains that spec-driven development can be done manually with any assistant or via open-source tools like Spec It. Kiro offers spec mode in the IDE and plan mode in the CLI. Works for both greenfield and legacy projects; also has a bug fix spec mode.

sections.title: Requirements and Design Documents
sections.summary: Details the requirements phase in EARS format with clarifying Q&A and quick plan mode. Describes the design document phase with mermaid diagrams and ASCII art. Recommends stopping to inject your own expertise and taste into the documents before proceeding.

sections.title: Implementation Phase and Property-Based Tests
sections.summary: Covers reviewing markdown files for inconsistencies, hallucinations, and errors. The implementation phase produces a task list with property-based tests validating against requirements and design documents. Hanchett recommends asking the AI to create an MVP from the top four tasks first to see it working before full implementation.

sections.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration
sections.summary: Discusses MCP as a protocol for model providers to connect to external data sources. Despite internet skepticism, Hanchett believes MCP is still maturing with a long road ahead, especially around security. Key benefit: pulling requirements from Jira, Asana, or other project management tools into the spec-driven flow. Steering docs or agents.md can instruct the AI to use specific MCP servers.

sections.title: Kiro IDE Demo: Movie Database Project
sections.summary: Demos Kiro on a greenfield movie database project. Shows a design document with mermaid sequence diagrams, property-based tests using fast-check in TypeScript running dozens to hundreds of times, EARS-format requirements (movie data loading, filter engine), and a task list where tasks 1-4 deliver a working MVP with browsable movie grid, search, genre filtering, sorting, and 80s synthwave theme. Closes with links to kiro.dev, Discord, LinkedIn, Blue Sky, and X.
